en: Besides the Single Responsibility Principle
and the Open-Closed Principle, which are
the 2 most important principles for us here
when it comes to writing clean code, we also
have 3 other principles.
And I wanna next dive into the Liskov
Substitution Principle
because even though these remaining 3
principles are not as important for writing
clean code as the first 2, I still wanna
cover this entire list.
So what's the Liskov Substitution Principle
all about then?
The Liskov Substitution Principle basically
says that objects should be replaceable with
instances of their subclasses
without altering their behavior.
Now this is a very abstract sentence. What
exactly does it mean?
Here I again got an example.
We have a class Bird, let's say.
Of course, this is a very simple example
here, but we got a class Bird which has a
fly method.
We then got a class Eagle which extends the
Bird class and adds a dive method because
not all birds really can dive. Eagles though
certainly can dive down onto their prey.
And then here we got some code where I
instantiate Bird not Eagle but Bird and call
fly.
And the
Liskov Substitution Principle now basically
says
that I should be able to substitute Bird
down there
with a subclass of this Bird superclass.
So here we should be able to instantiate an
Eagle instead
and call fly on an Eagle and we should
essentially have the same behavior as
before.
So of course, in a real program, the Eagle
class then might be doing more things than
just the Bird class.
I mean, even here we can see that we can
call dive in addition to fly,
but we still can call fly as before on the
Bird, and we can still expect that fly does
the same thing.
So in this example, the Bird flies.
In a real application, we could have
different databases, and no matter if it's
an SQL or MongoDB database, we should have a
connect method which always has the same
behavior of connecting to that database.
So it seems like everything is fine here,
right?
Well, what happens if we add a Penguin class
which also extends Bird?
A Penguin is a Bird. The problem just is
that a Penguin can't fly.
So we have the wrong
base class here, the wrong superclass.
Bird is a good superclass if we only work
with eagles and other birds who can fly,
but as soon as we start adding birds who
can't fly, we have a problem.
And if I have a look at this other example I
briefly mentioned where we maybe have
multiple databases which all have a connect
method,
even there, as soon as we add a database
which doesn't need to connect, let's say
some in-memory database, we also have the
problem of modeling our data and our
entities in the wrong way.
Because that's what the Liskov Substitution
Principle ultimately is all about. It wants
to ensure that you don't model your data in
the wrong way.
For example, here we picked a bird as a base
class for all our specialized birds and as
it turns out at the example of the penguin,
that was the wrong choice.
So how would you write proper code here?
Well, for example, you could add another
base class, let's say a FlyingBird,
which actually has this fly method.
And it's the FlyingBird
which acts as a base class for the Eagle,
and it's the regular Bird which might have
other shared functionalities— it doesn't
here, but it could have—
which you use as a base class for the
Penguin.
And now indeed here you can use FlyingBird
and call fly
or use an Eagle and still call fly,
but you can't use a Penguin. And you also
don't need to substitute your FlyingBird or
Eagle with a Penguin because Penguin extends
Bird, not FlyingBird. The base class, the
superclass is a different one.
So that's what the Liskov Substitution
Principle is all about. If a class inherits
from another class, then you need to be able
to replace replace that other superclass
with instances of the inheriting class
without changing any behavior. And at the
example of a Penguin, that didn't work
unless we added a new superclass for Eagle
and all other birds who can fly because now
we can substitute these classes with each
other and we can substitute Bird with
Penguin because fly is not built into
Penguin.
So the Liskov Substitution Principle
ultimately is about forcing you to model
your data correctly.
Now, why is it not a super important
principle when it comes to writing clean
code?
Well, it certainly is important when it
comes to modeling data correctly, which of
course is an important part of writing good
and extensible code.
But from a readability and clean code
perspective,
I think it's fair to say that throughout
this example here and me adding this
FlyingBird class, the readability didn't
really change. It always was very readable
and understandable, and therefore the Liskov
Substitution Principle doesn't add too much
when it comes to just code readability and
clean code being written.
